summary:
Mars Pathfinder is an interactive Martian surface navigation and survival decision-support prototype designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Integrating official NASA Mars Trek WMTS layers—including MRO HiRISE, CTX, and MGS MOLA elevation/roughness mosaics—the platform enables route planning and risk analysis between Midway Base and Jezero Crater.

To address the challenges of steep slopes, craters, loose dunes, and fragmented mission datasets, Mars Pathfinder unifies geospatial mapping with hazard logging, slope threshold checks, and alternative pathfinding. The system evaluates route-hazard intersections, incorporates astronaut and equipment readiness profiles, and supports bidirectional mission history and CSV/JSON data exports.   

Unlike standard map viewers that only optimize for distance, Mars Pathfinder is built on a core principle: the shortest path is not always the safest, and the human factor is just as critical as terrain data. By integrating astronaut readiness and equipment checks directly into route validation, our prototype ensures safer, evidence-based exploration for future planetary missions.
details:
Mars Pathfinder is an interactive planetary surface navigation and survival decision-support prototype that integrates safe route planning, hazard assessment, and human-centered operational oversight across unexplored Martian terrain, specifically focusing on the exploration corridor between Midway Base and Jezero Crater. The system operates by unifying official NASA Mars Trek WMTS scientific datasets—including Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE and CTX), Mars Global Surveyor (MOLA topography and surface roughness), and Viking global mosaics—into a single geospatial interface. Users can delineate routes directly on the Martian surface and log environmental hazards such as dunes, boulders, craters, and steep slopes along with coordinates, estimated impact radii, and verifiable evidence sources. A built-in spatial analysis engine computes route-hazard intersections, evaluates critical slope thresholds (8° and 15°), and generates safe alternative pathways that bypass recorded obstacles. Furthermore, an integrated astronaut and equipment readiness module monitors self-reported fatigue, remaining mission duration, and gear status, automatically suspending route execution clearance whenever human or technical parameters exceed safe operational limits.

This integrated architecture consolidates fragmented orbital and surface datasets from multiple NASA missions into a cohesive workspace, accelerating multi-layered decision-making and mitigating navigational uncertainty. Grounded in the guiding principle that "the shortest path is not always the safest," the platform prioritizes gentle slope transitions and hazard avoidance over raw geometric distance, thereby enhancing mission survivability. In addition, bidirectional historical analysis—enabling cross-queries across routes, astronaut profiles, and hazards—combined with structured CSV and JSON import/export capabilities ensures full data provenance and scientific reproducibility. Consequently, the intended impact of Mars Pathfinder is twofold: it establishes a transparent, evidence-based decision-support framework for future human and robotic planetary exploration, while simultaneously serving as an accessible STEM education environment where students and emerging researchers can engage with authentic NASA geospatial data to test hypotheses and practice systematic risk management.

From a software and hardware architecture perspective, Mars Pathfinder is engineered as a lightweight, self-contained web application built entirely within a single portable HTML5 document utilizing CSS3 and modern JavaScript (ES6+), eliminating the need for external server infrastructure, database administration, or specialized hardware. For spatial visualization and geodetic calculations, the open-source Leaflet.js mapping library was specifically customized to replace Earth-centric Web Mercator projections with an equirectangular coordinate reference system (L.CRS.Simple) calibrated to Mars's planetary radius ($R = 3,389.5\text{ km}$). While visual layers dynamically stream from official NASA Mars Trek WMTS endpoints (MRO HiRISE, CTX, MGS MOLA, and Viking mosaics) alongside NASA PDS atmospheric archive references, persistent mission logs are stored locally within standard desktop and tablet web browsers via localStorage. The creativity of the project lies in bridging geospatial terrain intelligence with human-factor telemetry inside a unified safety gate, departing from conventional mapping tools that merely compute the shortest geometric path. Beyond generating obstacle-avoiding alternative routes, the system actively prevents human error under pressure by locking new route execution whenever self-reported crew fatigue, remaining mission time, or equipment readiness crosses critical safety thresholds. Throughout the engineering process, our team carefully accounted for planetary geodetic fidelity, strict epistemic transparency—distinguishing unverified student observations (reported) from evidence-backed measurements (verified)—portable offline data backups (CSV/JSON), and operational resilience through automated fallback layer switching during network interruptions.
